pos: n. (the Hanseatic city at the mouth of the Daugava; the first city of the Baltic east to receive the Reformation)
etymology: Of disputed origin, probably from Livonian ringa, a bend or loop in a river; first recorded in Latin as Riga.
biblical_def: Riga was founded in 1201 by Bishop Albert of Bremen as the base of the crusade against the Livonian tribes, and grew into the great Hanseatic port of the eastern Baltic. The Reformation reached it through its merchants and its two parish pulpits: Andreas Knopken began lecturing on Romans in St Peter's in 1521 and held a public disputation in 1522, and Sylvester Tegetmeier came the same year to St James's. The town council took the city evangelical over the archbishop's opposition. In 1524 a crowd stripped the churches of their images, and in 1530 the city received a church ordinance drafted with Bugenhagen's and Briesmann's help, so that order followed disorder rather than the reverse. Riga was afterwards contested between Poland, Sweden and Russia for two centuries and kept its Lutheran church through all of it. The dictionary records it as the type of a trading city where the word was preached in the open: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” (Pro 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mart as a place of public traffic, a market; a street as a paved way or road in a city; and a disputation as a contest in argument, a controversy in words.
webster_full: MART, n. A place of public traffic or sale; a market; a fair; a place of great commerce.
STREET, n. [Saxon straet.] Properly, a paved way or road; a way in a city or village broader than a lane or alley.
DISPUTATION, n. [L. disputatio.] A contest in words; a controversy carried on in argument; an exercise in colleges.
ORDINANCE, n. [L. ordino.] A rule established by authority; a law, statute or decree; a permanent rule of action.
COUNCIL, n. [L. concilium.] An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation or advice.
scriptures: Pro 1:20
Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets:
Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him.
And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
Jer 5:1

Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know, and seek in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man, if there be any that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth; and I will pardon it.
corruption_summary: The Hanseatic city at the mouth of the Daugava, taken evangelical by its council in the 1520s against the archbishop, with Knopken at St Peter's and Tegetmeier at St James's.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty is that Riga's Reformation was a German burghers' reformation in a city whose Latvian-speaking majority were servants, carters and labourers outside the guilds. The preaching was in German; the images came down in German churches; the ordinance was for a German council. Latvian did not get its Scriptures for another century and a half. The dictionary records the gain without pretending the gospel went in that generation to the people of the land.

The principle to recover is that the word belongs out of doors, in the market and the street, and not only in the lecture room. Wisdom is pictured as a public crier with no appointment: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets” (Pro 1:20). Paul works both the synagogue and the market, daily, with whoever turns up — “and in the market daily with them that met with him” (Act 17:17) — and then settles for eighteen months of plain teaching when a city will have it (Act 18:11). Jeremiah is sent through the streets to look for one righteous man (Jer 5:1), which is what a preacher in a trading city is actually doing.

pos: n. (the land of the eastern Baltic held by the Teutonic knights, reformed in the 1520s and destroyed by war in the 1560s)
etymology: From the tribal name of the Livs, a Finnic people of the coast; latinised Livonia, the land of the Livs.
biblical_def: Livonia was the territory of modern Latvia and Estonia, conquered in the thirteenth century by the Sword Brethren and then the Teutonic Order and governed as a confederation of the Order, the Archbishop of Riga, three other bishops, and the towns — five or six jealous powers in one small land. The Reformation entered through Riga, Reval and Dorpat in the 1520s and was adopted by the towns and much of the nobility within a decade, while the ecclesiastical princes resisted and lost. The confederation then fell apart: the Livonian War of 1558 to 1583 broke the Order, partitioned the land between Poland, Sweden and Denmark, and left the countryside wrecked. Courland survived as a Lutheran duchy. The dictionary records Livonia as the clearest instance in Europe of a church planted by conquest which could not hold what the sword had taken: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crusade as a military expedition undertaken for the recovery of the Holy Land, hence any religious war; carnal as fleshly, pertaining to the flesh rather than the spirit; and a confederation as a league, a union of states.
webster_full: CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land; any romantic undertaking under a religious pretext.
CARNAL, a. [L. carnalis.] Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to the spirit and its influences.
CONFEDERATION, n. A league; a compact for mutual support; a union of states by agreement.
MIGHT, n. Strength; force; power; ability to act with effect.
SWORD, n. An offensive weapon worn at the side; the emblem of war, of justice, and of authority.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
corruption_summary: The eastern Baltic land held by the Teutonic Order, reformed through its towns in the 1520s and partitioned between Poland, Sweden and Denmark in the Livonian War.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a live and serious argument to face: that Livonia proves Christianity in northern Europe was simply a conquest, with the cross used as a flag. The dictionary does not dodge it. The Baltic crusades were wars of conquest; the Order took land, labour and tribute; the peasantry were made serfs by Christian lords and stayed serfs under Lutheran ones. What the record also shows is that two and a half centuries of armed Christianisation had not produced a people who could read the Scriptures, and that it was the preachers, not the knights, who set about that.

The principle to recover is that the kingdom does not advance by the means a state uses. Zechariah says it to a man rebuilding with every political reason to rely on a patron: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). Paul grants that the warfare is real and insists the weapons are of a different kind — “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). The Lord disarms Peter with a general law, not a special case: “for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).

“for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — the confederation broken in the Livonian War, 1558 to 1583.

pos: n. (c. 1468–1539; the reformer of Riga, called the apostle of Livonia)
etymology: Knopken, a Low German surname from Knopf, a knob or button; Andreas, from Greek andreios, manly.
biblical_def: Andreas Knopken was born in Pomerania, taught in Bugenhagen's school at Treptow, and went to Riga about 1517 as a chaplain before returning to Treptow and then coming back to Riga for good in 1521. He began lecturing publicly on the Epistle to the Romans in St Peter's, printed his notes on it, and on 12 June 1522 defended twenty-four theses in a public disputation before the council and clergy. No one answered him effectively, and the council appointed him archdeacon of St Peter's, where he preached until his death in 1539. He wrote Riga's first evangelical liturgy and, with Briesmann, its church ordinance; he restrained the iconoclasts in 1524 and opposed the radicals as firmly as he opposed Rome. Called the apostle of Livonia, he began where Paul began: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an archdeacon as an ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop; a thesis as a position or proposition laid down and maintained; and the gospel as the history of the birth, life and doctrines of Christ, good tidings.
webster_full: ARCHDEACON, n. [Gr. archos, chief, and deacon.] In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop, who has jurisdiction over the clergy of a district.
THESIS, n. [Gr. thesis, a position.] A position or proposition which a person advances and offers to maintain by argument.
GOSPEL, n. [Saxon godspell, good tidings.] The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ; the doctrine of salvation by Christ.
DETERMINE, v.t. [L. determino.] To fix the limits of; to resolve; to settle a purpose in the mind.
INSTANT, a. Pressing; urgent; importunate; immediate; without intervening time.
scriptures: Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Act 18:9
Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
corruption_summary: Reformer of Riga: lectured on Romans in St Peter's from 1521, defended twenty-four theses in the disputation of June 1522, and served as archdeacon there until 1539.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Knopken is instead a standing correction to a bad habit of our own. He is remembered, where he is remembered, for a single dramatic disputation; what he actually did was lecture through Romans, print the exposition, then preach in one pulpit for seventeen years and write the liturgy his congregation would use after he was gone. The disputation was the public moment. The exposition and the ordinance were the work.

The principle to recover is that the gospel preached expositionally is itself the power, and needs no supplement. Paul grounds his own confidence not in his gifts but in the message's nature: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16). He narrows his subject on purpose — “For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2) — and the charge to Timothy is for all weathers, with longsuffering built in: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). To a man in a hostile city the Lord says simply, “Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace” (Act 18:9).

pos: n. (d. 1552; preacher at St James's in Riga, the fiercer of the city's two reformers)
etymology: Tegetmeier, a Low German occupational surname, a Meier or steward of a Teget holding; Sylvester, from Latin silvestris, of the woods.
biblical_def: Sylvester Tegetmeier was a Rostock man who studied there and at Wittenberg and came to Riga in 1522 to preach at St James's. Where Knopken taught, Tegetmeier denounced. He preached against the images, the mass and the monasteries in terms the crowds understood immediately, and in March 1524 a mob went through the Riga churches and destroyed the images and altars; Tegetmeier had preached the sermons that lit it, and the councils of the city spent years repairing the damage to its order and its own legitimacy. He later quarrelled with Knopken and with the council, and served at St James's until his death in 1552. The dictionary records him because the second commandment is true and the riot was still wrong, and the two have to be said together: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4), and “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an image as a representation of a person or thing, an idol; iconoclast as a breaker or destroyer of images; and decently as in a becoming manner, with propriety of behaviour.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. [L. imago.] A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; an idol; the object of idolatrous worship.
ICONOCLAST, n. [Gr. eikon, an image, and klao, to break.] A breaker or destroyer of images; one who opposes the worship of images.
DECENTLY, adv. In a decent or becoming manner; with propriety of behaviour; without immodesty.
ZEAL, n. [Gr. zelos.] Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; enthusiasm; it may be good or bad according to its object.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition; methodical arrangement; established mode of proceeding; rule.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Preacher at St James's in Riga from 1522 whose sermons touched off the iconoclasm of March 1524; quarrelled with Knopken and with the council; died 1552.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does have to hold two things that are usually separated. Tegetmeier was right about the images: the second commandment forbids them in worship, and the Riga churches were full of objects men had been taught to venerate. He was wrong about the mob. A congregation turned loose on its own building has not obeyed the commandment; it has substituted its own zeal for the magistrate's duty and the church's order, and it taught Riga's council for a generation to associate the gospel with wreckage.

The principle to recover is that both halves are commanded. God's refusal to share his glory with an artefact is absolute and his own: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8), and the idols are weighed for what they are — “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4). But the reform of worship is itself to be a reform, not a riot: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Zeal that will not wait for order is not obedience in a hurry; it is a different sin.

pos: n. (d. 1532; Riga preacher, the first to put Scripture and psalmody into Latvian)
etymology: Ramm, a Low German surname from Ram, a ram or battering ram; Nicolaus, from Greek Nikolaos, conqueror of the people.
biblical_def: Nicolaus Ramm was a preacher at Riga in the first evangelical generation, serving the Latvian-speaking congregation of St James's and, after about 1527, St Jacob's chapel. He is the first man known to have turned any part of the Scriptures into Latvian: a rendering of the Ten Commandments, and a verse translation of the hymn Nun freut euch, lieben Christen g'mein, both for the use of the Latvian labourers and carters who had been baptised for three centuries without being taught in their own tongue. The texts are lost except in fragments quoted by later writers. He died in 1532, and Latvian would wait until Glück's Bible of 1689 for a complete Scripture. The dictionary records him because he began it, and because the new song in Revelation is sung in every tongue there is: “And they sung a new song” (Rev 5:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song or hymn; a tongue as a language, the speech of a nation; and wonderful as adapted to excite wonder or astonishment.
webster_full: PSALM, n. [Gr. psalmos.] A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse designed to be sung in the worship of God.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; a language; the speech or dialect of a particular people.
WONDERFUL, a. Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; marvellous.
KINDRED, n. Relation by birth; relatives by blood; a family, a tribe, a race.
NEW, a. Lately made, invented or produced; not before known; recently come into being.
scriptures: Rev 5:9

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;
Psa 96:1
O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth.
Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
corruption_summary: Riga preacher to the Latvian congregation who made the first Latvian renderings of the Ten Commandments and of a Reformation hymn; died 1532.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a hard fact in Ramm's entry rather than a corruption: three hundred years of nominal Christianity in Livonia had produced no Latvian catechism, no Latvian psalm, and no Latvian Scripture, and the first attempt at any of them is a few lost pages from a city preacher in the 1520s. That is an indictment of the conquering church, and the dictionary states it plainly rather than treating Ramm as a charming footnote.

The principle to recover is that the song of the redeemed is multilingual by purchase, not by concession. The new song in heaven names the reason it is sung in every speech: Christ “hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9). The command to sing is addressed to all the earth and not to one nation — “O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth” (Psa 96:1) — and the praise has a congregation, not a soloist (Psa 149:1). At Pentecost the wonderful works of God are heard in the hearers' own tongues (Act 2:11), which settles what a Latvian carter was owed.

pos: n. (the Baltic duchy west of the Daugava, Lutheran from its founding in 1561 and the one piece of Livonia that survived the wars)
etymology: From the tribal name of the Curonians, latinised Curonia, with German Land; the land of the Curs.
biblical_def: Courland is the western part of modern Latvia, between the Daugava and the sea. When the Livonian confederation collapsed under Russian attack, the last Master of the Livonian Order, Gotthard Kettler, submitted to Poland in 1561, dissolved the Order, and took Courland and Semgallia as a hereditary Lutheran duchy for himself and his heirs. He got what Albert of Prussia had got thirty-six years earlier and by much the same means. The duchy lasted until 1795 and was consistently Lutheran: Kettler's ordinances of 1567 required a church and a school in every parish, the visitations enforced them, and a Curonian peasantry that had been nominally Christian for three centuries began to be catechised. Courland is the small, durable survival out of a general wreck. Proverbs gives the test by which such a state is measured: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a duchy as the territory of a duke; a visitation as the official visit of a superior to inspect the state of a church or district; and authority as legal power, the right to command.
webster_full: DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; the official visit of a superior to a church or district for the purpose of inspection and correction.
AUTHORITY, n. [L. auctoritas.] Legal power, or a right to command or to act; the power of a ruler.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the township committed to his charge.
REJOICE, v.i. To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations.
scriptures: Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him.
And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered.
corruption_summary: The Baltic duchy founded in 1561 when Gotthard Kettler dissolved the Livonian Order; Lutheran throughout, with a church and school required in every parish from 1567.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest reckoning with Courland is about serfdom. Kettler's ordinances gave every parish a church and a school, and the same century bound the Curonian and Latvian peasantry more tightly to the land than they had been under the Order. A duchy can require catechism in every village and still hold its catechumens as property, and Courland did. The dictionary records the schools as a real good and refuses to let them stand as the whole account.

The principle to recover is that rule is to be measured by what happens to the ruled. Proverbs supplies the test and it is not stability or revenue: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2). Paul states the ruler's proper direction — “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3) — and the ultimate subjection of every ruler is already written: “Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him” (Psa 72:11). Hezekiah is the standard of a prince's reform: he did it “with all his heart, and prospered” (2Ch 31:21).

pos: n. (1517–1587; last Master of the Livonian Order and first Duke of Courland, who established the Lutheran church there)
etymology: Gotthard, from Old High German got, God, and hart, hard or firm; Kettler, a Westphalian surname from Kessler, a kettle-maker.
biblical_def: Gotthard Kettler was a Westphalian nobleman who rose through the Livonian Order to become its last Master in 1559, at the moment Ivan IV's armies were tearing the country apart. Unable to defend it, he put Livonia under Polish protection in 1561, dissolved the Order, and retained Courland and Semgallia as a hereditary duchy, converting to Lutheranism and ruling until 1587. Judged as a soldier he lost a country; judged as a churchman he founded one of the better-ordered Lutheran establishments in the north. His church ordinances of 1567 required a church and a schoolhouse in every parish, provided stipends, ordered regular visitations, and had some seventy churches built. He also confirmed the nobility's hold over the peasantry, and the duchy's later history is of a strong gentry and a weak duke. The dictionary records him with Hezekiah's pattern in view: “opened the doors of the house of the LORD, and repaired them” (2Ch 29:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a master as a chief, the head of an order or society; to repair as to restore to a sound state what is partially decayed; and a stipend as a settled pay or compensation.
webster_full: MASTER, n. A chief, a head; one who rules or directs; the head of an order, society or school.
REPAIR, v.t. [L. reparo.] To restore to a sound or good state after decay or injury; to mend; to refit.
STIPEND, n. [L. stipendium.] Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily or monthly.
PERFECT, a. [L. perfectus.] Finished; complete; having all that is requisite; in Scripture, upright, sincere, without guile.
BUILD, v.t. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice; to raise by art; to establish.
scriptures: He in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the LORD, and repaired them.
And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
corruption_summary: Last Master of the Livonian Order, who dissolved it in 1561, became first Duke of Courland, and whose 1567 ordinances required a church and a school in every parish.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kettler is often written up as the man who sold a country for a crown, and the charge deserves a hearing rather than a dismissal. He was the last Master of a crusading order sworn to hold Livonia, and he ended by handing most of it to Poland, Sweden and Denmark and keeping a duchy for his family. The defence is that the Order was militarily finished before he took it and that the alternative to partition was Russian conquest of the whole. The dictionary lets both stand, and notes that he spent the duchy's first decades building churches rather than fortresses.

The principle to recover is that a prince's reform begins with the house of God and is measured by thoroughness. Hezekiah's reign opens with carpentry: “opened the doors of the house of the LORD, and repaired them” (2Ch 29:3), and the summary of his reign ties the public work to the inward motive — “to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered” (2Ch 31:21). Haggai rebukes the inversion of that order, panelled houses beside a ruined temple: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). And the ruler's own household is where the integrity is tested first (Psa 101:2).

pos: n. (the capital of the duchy of Courland, now Jelgava; seat of its ducal church, consistory and school)
etymology: From Latvian Jelgava, by way of Livonian jalgab, a town on the river; the German Mitau is of disputed derivation.
biblical_def: Mitau stands on the Lielupe in the middle of Courland and was the ducal residence from the founding of the duchy in 1561. It held the castle, the ducal church of Holy Trinity, the consistory that governed the Courland church, the gymnasium, and in due course the Academia Petrina. It was the place where the duchy's church business was done: ministers examined, parishes visited, ordinances published, and Latvian catechetical material prepared for the country parishes. The town was burned and taken repeatedly in the Swedish, Polish and Russian wars and rebuilt each time; its church records are among the fullest in the Baltic. The dictionary records Mitau as an ordinary administrative capital doing ordinary and necessary work, the sort of place Nehemiah's summons is actually addressed to: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consistory as an ecclesiastical court or assembly; a gymnasium as a place of exercise, in Germany a school of learning; and a reproach as censure mingled with contempt, shame.
webster_full: CONSISTORY, n. [L. consistorium.] A place of justice in a spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of church affairs.
GYMNASIUM, n. [Gr. gumnasion.] A place of exercise; in Germany, a school or seminary of the higher kind.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; abuse; shame; disgrace; infamy.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place; the place of abode; a seat.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation; a fortress; a citadel.
scriptures: Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
corruption_summary: Ducal capital of Courland from 1561, now Jelgava; seat of the castle, the Holy Trinity church, the consistory that governed the Courland church, and its schools.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a quiet error the entry exists to rebut: that church administration is the dull residue of real religion, and that a consistory and a set of parish visitation records are not where anything important happened. In Courland they are exactly where it happened. Whether a village had a schoolmaster, whether its minister could preach in Latvian, whether a catechism had reached it — those questions were answered at Mitau, in writing, year by year, and the answers decided what that village knew of God.

The principle to recover is that building and repairing are spiritual work and are commanded as such. Nehemiah's appeal is practical to the point of being unromantic, and he grounds it in the dishonour done to God's name by ruins: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). The Psalm sends the worshipper on an inspection tour and tells him to count — “Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof” (Psa 48:12). Haggai names the sin of seeing to one's own comfort while the house lies waste (Hag 1:4). An archive of visitations is obedience in ledger form.

pos: n. (c. 1471–1527; Archbishop of Riga, who fought the Reformation in Livonia and lost)
etymology: Blankenfeld, a German surname from blank, white or bright, and Feld, field; the white field.
biblical_def: Johann Blankenfeld came of a Berlin patrician family, took doctorates in both laws at Bologna, and rose through the Livonian church as Bishop of Reval, then of Dorpat, and from 1524 Archbishop of Riga, holding all three sees at once for a time. He spent his archiepiscopate trying to stop the Reformation: he pressed the Emperor and the Pope for mandates against the Riga preachers, worked to bring the Order and the towns into a Catholic front, and was suspected of inviting Moscow's help against his own city. The Order arrested him in 1525 at Ronneburg; he was released after renouncing his foreign dealings, set out for the Emperor to argue his case, and died at Torda in Transylvania in 1527. The archbishopric did not recover. The dictionary records him as the Baltic's instance of Gamaliel's warning being ignored: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God” (Act 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an archbishop as a chief bishop having jurisdiction over other bishops; to overthrow as to demolish, to subvert, to destroy; and vain as empty, worthless, having no substance or value.
webster_full: ARCHBISHOP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class; a metropolitan bishop who superintends the conduct of other bishops.
OVERTHROW, v.t. To turn upside down; to demolish; to subvert; to destroy; to defeat.
VAIN, a. [L. vanus.] Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; deliberation; a plan or purpose formed; the design of God.
PLACE, n. A particular portion of space; station; office; rank; a dwelling.
scriptures: Act 5:39
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.
corruption_summary: Archbishop of Riga from 1524 who held three Livonian sees, petitioned Emperor and Pope against the Reformation, was arrested by the Order in 1525, and died in 1527.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Honesty requires two admissions. Blankenfeld was not a fool or a monster: he was a trained canonist defending an office and an order he held to be of divine institution, in a province visibly falling apart, and some of his fears about what would follow were justified. And the dictionary should not pretend the charge against him of seeking Russian intervention against Riga is proven; it was alleged by his enemies and he denied it. What is certain is that he spent his whole archiepiscopate on external force — mandates, alliances, arrests — and never once on an answer to Knopken's exposition of Romans.

The principle to recover is that an institution cannot be defended against God by procedure. Gamaliel's caution is addressed to men with full legal authority over the preachers in front of them: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God” (Act 5:39). Proverbs puts the limit absolutely — “There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD” (Pro 21:30). And the council in John shows what the calculation looks like from inside, when a man weighs his place and nation against the truth of what is happening: “If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him” (Joh 11:48).

pos: n. (the Livonian castle-town, now Cesis; residence of the Order's Masters and the scene of its last defence in 1577)
etymology: From German Wenden, the Wends, a name for the Slavic and Baltic peoples east of the Elbe; the Latvian Cesis is of local origin.
biblical_def: Wenden was the strongest inland castle in Livonia and the usual residence of the Masters of the Livonian Order from the fourteenth century. The Reformation reached it with the rest of the land in the 1520s; the Order's own chapel became a Lutheran parish church, and the Masters buried there lie under a reformed roof. In 1577 Ivan IV's army besieged the castle. When the walls were about to be carried, the remnant of the garrison and the townspeople who had taken refuge in the keep gathered in the powder magazine and blew it and themselves up rather than be taken alive. The castle was never rebuilt and the ruin stands. The dictionary records Wenden because the strongest fortress in the country is the place where a whole history of trusting in walls came to its end: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fortress as a fortified place, a strong hold; a tower as a building raised to a considerable elevation, a fortress; and to trust as to place confidence in, to rely on.
webster_full: FORTRESS, n. [L. fortis, strong.] Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a strong hold.
TOWER, n. A building raised to a considerable elevation; a citadel; a fortress; figuratively, a defence.
TRUST, v.i. To place confidence in; to rely on; to depend upon with assurance.
CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a car; in antiquity, a vehicle used in war, drawn by horses.
STRONG HOLD, n. A fastness; a fort; a fortified place; a place of security.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: The Livonian Order's chief inland castle and residence of its Masters, now Cesis; its garrison blew up the keep rather than surrender to Ivan IV in 1577.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The end of Wenden is told two ways and both are used badly. One makes the garrison heroes of a last stand; the other makes them suicides. The dictionary will not resolve a thing it cannot judge: men and women in a keep about to fall to an army with a known record of what it did to prisoners are in a position no comfortable verdict reaches. What can be said is that the castle had been the strongest thing in Livonia for two hundred and fifty years and it did not save them, and that the Order which built it had staked everything on exactly that kind of strength.

The principle to recover is the contrast the Psalm draws, which is not between weakness and strength but between two objects of trust: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The alternative is not fortlessness; it is a different fortress: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). Jeremiah puts a curse on the inversion — “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5) — and Paul names which strongholds actually come down (2Co 10:4).
